SK2170 The indentation says the statement is in the body and it is not

An if, else, while, for, foreach, lock, using or fixed has a single unbraced statement as its body, and the next statement is indented as far as that body or further, so the layout claims a block the grammar does not give.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

if (stale) Reload(); Publish(); Publish() runs every time. Nothing about the program says so, and everything about the picture says the opposite — which is the whole failure: the reader's eye takes indentation as structure and C# does not. ⚠ This is the one half of the concept the compiler leaves alone, and that was measured rather than assumed. The other half — an empty statement standing in for a body, if (x); { … } — is CS0642, on by default, and it reaches further than doc 17 supposed: it covers if, else, lock, do, using and fixed outright, and covers while, for and foreach exactly when a block follows the ;, which is precisely the shape that misleads. So this rule declines an empty body followed by a block and reports one followed by anything else — while (x), then ; on its own line, then a statement aligned with the ; is a real finding the compiler is silent about. ⚠ The first draft declined every empty body and a sabotage proved the exemption unreachable, because while (x) ; puts the ; on the header's own line, which the line test already declines. ⚠ Indentation is not structure anywhere in C#, so nothing but a formatter is looking at it, and Skala is a formatter: the rule reads the leading whitespace of three lines and compares them as strings, which is a question no semantic model can be asked.

Example

Instead of:

if (stale)
    Reload();
    Publish();

Write:

if (stale) {
    Reload();
    Publish();
}

// or, if `Publish()` really was meant to be unconditional, written so it reads that way:
if (stale)
    Reload();

Publish();

When it does not fire

⚠ Indentation is compared as a string prefix, never as a column number, and that is what makes the rule safe in a tab-indented file. The header's indent must be a proper prefix of the body's, and the next statement's must equal the body's exactly; a file indented with tabs compares tab prefixes and a file indented with spaces compares space prefixes, and a line that mixes them fails the prefix test and is declined rather than guessed at. A column count would call one tab and one space the same depth and report a file that is merely inconsistent. ⚠ Alignment, not "at least as deep", and the corpus is what settled it. The looser test reports four times on unformatted/scramble/, a slice whose whitespace has been randomised on purpose: there the following statement lands 2, 4 or 6 columns past the body, which reads as mangled or as a continuation rather than as a sibling, and asking for the column a reader would actually see declines all four. ⚠ Three lines, three separate requirements, and dropping any one of them over-fires. The control statement must begin its own line, the body must begin a later line indented deeper than the header, and the next statement must begin a later line still, indented to exactly the body's column. if (x) A(); B(); on one line has no layout to mislead anyone; if (x)\n A();\nB(); is correctly outdented and is the shape the rule exists to leave alone. ⚠ A braced body is never examined, because a block cannot lie about what it contains. ⚠ An empty body is examined, but only where `CS0642` is silent. The compiler reports an empty loop body when a block follows the ; and not otherwise, so a not-a-block statement aligned with the ; is this rule's and a block is the compiler's; the guard is that narrow overlap and a fixture reaches it from each side. ⚠ The trailing embedded statement is what is measured, so an `else` is followed down: in if (a)\n A();\nelse\n B();\n C(); the body compared against C() is B(), not A(). A do is excluded, because its body is not trailing — the while follows it — so nothing below can be misread as belonging to it. ⚠ A preprocessor directive anywhere between the body and the next statement withdraws the finding: under an #if the two lines are not necessarily both in the program, and the indentation of a conditionally compiled region is a convention rather than a claim. ⚠ The rule reads the trivia of the tree as parsed — the source as the author wrote it — exactly as SK2063 does, and like SK2063 it can be silenced by running the formatter, which re-indents the second statement to the truth. That is not a defect in the rule; it is the repair, applied by a different command. There is no fix, because the two repairs — brace the body, or outdent the statement — are different programs and the code contains no signal for which was meant. Generated code is excluded.
